text: So quick context, this is an all-female British chess team called She Plays To Win. They have just been promoted to Division 1 of the Four Nations Chess League of Britain and Ireland. Division 1 has a long-standing rule that every team must include at least one male and one female player. So their all-female lineup will now have to include at least one man. And I actually understand part of their complaint. The rule was introduced largely because chess is overwhelmingly male and the idea was to guarantee women opportunities to play. So yes, there is something counterintuitive about using a rule designed to increase female participation in a situation where you already have an entirely female team. But here's where you lose me. First, I actually checked the rules, because from this interview you could easily get the impression that one of these women now has to be kicked off the team. That's not actually the case. Division 1 matches are played on 8 boards, but teams can register squads of up to 16 players. So they can keep all 8 women and simply add a male player to the squad. Now yes, whenever that man plays, one of the women would have to sit that particular match out because only 8 people can play at once. But nobody has to be kicked off the team. Second, this rule did not suddenly appear because an all-female team got promoted. It has explicitly required both male and female representation for decades. This was a long-standing, publicly available rule of the division they were trying to reach. And this is where I struggle with the fairness argument. When an otherwise all-male lineup is told, sorry, you cannot play 8 men, you need to include a woman, that is treated as a positive rule encouraging female participation. But now, in the rare situation where the exact same rule works the other way around, suddenly it is unfair and a step backwards, that is where the double standard becomes pretty obvious. And ladies, you are chess players, aren't you supposed to calculate several moves ahead? Because suppose your campaign succeeds and the league responds by removing the sex requirement entirely. Great, you can field 8 women, but every other team can now field 8 men. And considering how heavily male competitive chess still is, what do you think is going to happen more often? All-female teams suddenly appearing across division 1? Or male-dominated teams no longer having to give one of their 8 playing spots to a woman? You might save one female playing spot on your own team and, as an unintended consequence, contribute to considerably fewer women playing across the rest of the league. Now, there is another option, of course. They could change the rule to say every team needs at least one woman, but there is no requirement to include a man. That would actually fit the original purpose of the policy. But then, let's call it what it is, an explicitly unequal rule designed to increase female participation. You can make an argument for that, but what you cannot really do is call the current rule fair when it forces men to make room for women, and then call the exact same rule unfair the moment women have to make room for one man. Fairness cannot just mean fairness when it benefits you.
